import re

# Negated class: one character that is not in the menu.
print(re.findall(r"[^aeiou ]", "lexer rules"))           # every consonant
print(re.fullmatch(r"#[^\n]*", "# note\nx = 1"))          # None: the class cannot cross the newline
print(re.match(r"#[^\n]*", "# note\nx = 1").group())      # the comment stops at the newline

# A class excludes characters, not a sequence.
by_class     = r"/\*[^*/]*\*/"
by_lookahead = r"/\*(?:(?!\*/).)*\*/"
for c in ["/* plain */", "/* a * b */", "/* x / y */", "/* one */ two */"]:
    print(f"{c!r:20} class={bool(re.fullmatch(by_class, c))!s:5} lookahead={bool(re.fullmatch(by_lookahead, c))}")

# A whole line with no TODO anywhere in it.  Case matters.
for line in ["x = 1", "# TODO: fix", "y = 2  # todo later"]:
    print(f"{line!r:22} {bool(re.fullmatch(r'(?!.*TODO).*', line))}")
description: This example contrasts negated character classes with negative lookaheads for excluding text.

steps.description: The negated class at line 4 finds characters that are not vowels or spaces. The comment pattern excludes newlines, so its match stops before one.
by_class excludes every individual * and / in a comment body. by_lookahead instead checks that the two-character closing delimiter does not start at each position.

steps.answer: The lookahead pattern accepts it because a lone * does not begin the closing delimiter */.
steps.question: Which pattern accepts '/* a * b */'?

steps.description: The final pattern uses a negative lookahead to reject a full line containing uppercase TODO. The test also shows that this match is case-sensitive.
The program prints the class and lookahead results for each candidate block comment.
